observation.visible_scene: High aerial view looking across a thick sea of low fog/cloud that fills the lower two-thirds of the frame. On the right, a city skyline (mid- and high-rise buildings, a thin antenna mast) rises above the fog line; on the far left edge a gilded Orthodox-style onion dome with a small white tower base sits close to the camera. The upper portion is clear pale-blue sky.
visible_changes: The gilded dome and white tower base on the left progressively slide out of frame toward the left and downward, so that by the last frame only a tiny sliver of structure remains at the bottom-left corner; this is a change in framing (camera movement / parallax), not the dome itself moving.

As the foreground dome exits, the open fog surface on the left side of the frame becomes more exposed, and the right-side building cluster shifts slightly within the frame, consistent with a slow camera pan/truck to the right (and a small vertical shift).

The fog layer remains present and roughly level across the whole excerpt; its internal texture and the brighter patches within it change subtly from frame to frame, indicating gentle drifting/rolling of the cloud surface rather than a uniform translation.
The buildings, antenna and horizon line stay above the fog throughout; no building is newly revealed or swallowed by the fog within this segment.
Sky color and overall lighting stay essentially constant (clear, hazy daylight).
outside_clip_unknowns: The cause and direction of the camera motion (drone operator, pre-programmed path) are not shown.
Whether the fog is rising, dispersing, or stable in the long term is not determinable from this short window.
What lies below the fog and behind the camera is unseen.
The excerpt's endpoints are arbitrary; motion is already underway at t=0 and continues past the last frame.
uncertain_details: Exact camera motion vector: horizontal pan vs. lateral truck vs. slight tilt cannot be fully separated; background shift is small so the dominant cue is the foreground dome leaving frame.
The subtle changes in fog texture could be actual cloud drift or could partly result from the camera's parallax/angle change; the two cannot be cleanly distinguished here.
No clear physical interaction or onset/offset event is visible; the scene is a continuous slow reveal.
